facts.text: 23, Project Gatekeeper is creating a single sandboxed environment — running on the Army’s cloud but isolated from operationa l networks and sensitive data — where companies can bring their software for assessment, even if they don’t have an Army contract or a program manager to sponsor them.
Officials say Gatekeeper will cut the time required to get software approved fro m months to “minutes” — without sacrificing security in the process.
Compare that with the current, cumbersome clearance process that can take days or weeks — stalling some software projects for as long as nine months, Chiulli and other officials said.

That’s a long time to wait for a software upgrade, especially under a process that officials say lack consistent cybersecurity practices, transparency for contractors and visibility for Army leaders into what’s actually happening on their networks.
The service’s new cybersecurity testing sandbox will stand up on Oct.
That created a kind of Catch-22 : The companies best positioned to win Army software contracts where often the ones that already had them.

Meanwhile new, innovative entrants — the kind of companies that the Pentagon’s been courting for over a decade — struggled to navigate the combined complexities of cybersecurity rules, procurement regulations and Army bureaucracy.
In minutes, the automated system will either tell the company its software passed the test or give detailed, actionable feedback explaining why it failed.
Instead, they had to bring it onto an Army network and assess it there.
Companies will still need CAC cards to access the platform initially, officials acknowledged.
But the Army is finalizing an agreement with the General Services Administration (GSA) to use its Login.gov platform, which allows secure access to government systems for members of the public.

“The idea here is not to lessen the security requirements,” Wright emphasized, “but more to make the process more accessible and available, so that they can get immediate feedback and understand what it is that needs to be adjusted or corrected before these things are brought into an Army environment.”

“Success, to me, looks like a company, within minutes, is able to log in, submit their code and get the green check mark from our pipeline that says you are good to go,” acting Army Chief Information Officer Gabe Chiulli told reporters at the annual AUSA conference here this morning.

WASHINGTON — Some major Army software programs take six to eight months to establish an initial working capability, senior officials said Tuesday, describing delays the service hopes to reduce through a new system for evaluating commercial software.

Acting Army Chief Information Officer Gabriele "Gabe" Chiulli discusses Project Gatekeeper during a media roundtable at the Association of the United States Army's Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., Oct.
The Army plans to launch the software cybersecurity screening platform Oct.
23. (Photo by Ryan Thomas LaBee/Military.com)
The system uses established Army software security pipelines, including tools already used by other military services.
During the roundtable, Military.com asked how much money and manpower the Army expects to save by reducing the need to issue CACs to civilian developers.
Stay connected to your community and take full advantage of the Military.com experience by subscribing to the newsletter.
The Army has resorted to "weird janky things" to move software into its systems, he said.
Chiulli described the current process as a patchwork of procedures that can leave companies struggling to get software evaluated without already having access to military networks.
The Army is also working through how it will protect companies' proprietary code, particularly when they submit software before securing government contracts.
The initiative follows a broader Army effort to cut acquisition red tape and bring commercial technology to soldiers faster , which military leaders outlined earlier this year.
At launch, Gatekeeper will still require a Common Access Card, or CAC, the military credential that outside developers have often needed to work on government systems.

Gatekeeper is intended to replace those arrangements with a standardized testing process that lets developers identify vulnerabilities and correct them before moving software toward use on Army networks.
The platform will provide an isolated environment, separated from operational Army networks, where developers can upload software for conventional cybersecurity screening and an AI-assisted review.
